verbose

/ver-BOHS/ - the stress falls on BOHS · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Verbose means using far more words than the message needs — wordy to the point that the extra words bury the point.

Grandpa's voicemails are verbose: a full minute of weather, knee updates, and a review of lunch before the actual question finally arrives.

Example

The new hire's status emails were so verbose — every meeting recapped, every hallway chat footnoted — that her manager began skimming them for verbs. When she trimmed one down to its four real updates, replies came back within minutes.

Verbose is a charge about quantity: the emails' information was fine — four updates — but it arrived wrapped in ten times the words it needed, and that padding, not the ideas underneath it, is what verbose condemns.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

long-winded: Long-winded is the everyday complaint about talk that goes on far too long, usually tediously. Verbose is the more clinical charge, and it points at the words themselves: too many of them for the content, whether on the page or out loud.

rambling: Rambling faults the direction — talk that drifts from topic to topic with no plan or thread, and a rambling toast can be over in a minute. Verbose is strictly a charge about word count: more words than the message needs, however tidily they are organized.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

concise: saying it in the fewest words that still carry the meaning

succinct: compressed and to the point, with nothing wasted

Where it sits · how far the word count outruns the content

wordy → verbose → prolix

wordy vs. verbose: Wordy is the mild, everyday rung below verbose — a few more words than needed; verbose goes further, with padding heavy enough to start burying the point.

prolix vs. verbose: Prolix, this unit's own heavyweight, is stronger than verbose: verbose writing wastes words along the way, while prolix talk overruns its point so far that the listener loses the thread entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — verb: word (Latin verbum)

Suffix — ose: full of (Latin -osus)

Put it together: Latin verbum ('word') plus -osus ('full of') builds verbose: literally 'full of words.' The root runs a whole family about words through English — verbal, verbatim, adverb, proverb — and verbose is the branch that has too many of them.

Use the root in a new word: verbatim: The judge asked the clerk to read the disputed paragraph back verbatim before ruling on the objection.

Root Check

Word Choice

critical / editorial

Verbose is the plainest of this unit's charges against overwriting: it simply counts. Prolix adds tedium and a lost thread; turgid, the unit's adjective for swollen prose, adds self-importance; grandiloquence adds pomp. Verbose just says there are too many words for the content — which is why editors reach for it first.
